newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila bankers told to drop peso volatility band.
newsitem.headline: Manila bankers told to drop peso volatility band.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank on Sunday told the country's bankers to drop the volatility band rule when currency trading resumes on Monday, but said it was ready to step in if the peso suffered another steep fall.

Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), which controls currency trading among local banks, was discussing his proposal at a meeting late on Sunday.
"I will still be in the market," Singson told Reuters by telephone. "It doesn't mean that I will be completely out of the market...We will come in to calm down the market."
The volatility rule allows the BAP to temporarily halt trades if the peso moves above or below a 1.5 percent reference rate, which is the average rate of deals before trades were suspended.

Under the rule, the peso would open at 26.40 to the dollar at the resumption of trading on Monday despite plunging 11.5 percent to 29.40 pesos on Friday after the Central Bank allowed the currency to trade in a wider band in an effective devaluation.
"I suggested to them (the BAP) to take away the volatility band to give way to a whole and free interplay of market forces," Singson said, adding, "I suppose they will agree."
The Philippines was the second Asian country in two weeks to succumb to currency speculators, following in the footsteps of Thailand, which was forced into a de facto devaluation of the baht.

Before caving in, Manila's Central Bank spent an estimated $2 billion, or about 17 percent of the reserves it has left, and sent interest rates up to levels which analysts said would hurt the economy in a failed attempt to defend the peso.
Some bankers have said they believe keeping the volatility band rule will just sow confusion in the currency market, saying it is inconsistent with the Central Bank's new policy.
